title: EPIG-Tree: Compute-Optimal Branching for Gradient-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
trick: Spend forks where the ending depends most on which action is taken, weighted by how often the step is reached and how movable the policy is, per unit cost; estimate that dependence from a few pilot forks.
framing_stripped: Called compute-optimal branching by expected predictive information gain; it is an allocation rule for extra rollouts that targets the between-actions share of gradient variance, estimated from pilots.
load_bearing_assumption: Local value differences across actions can be estimated from a small pilot sample at a prefix (fails in sparse/non-smooth reward or tiny-action regimes, by their own admission).
weakest_component: The pilots: the quantity that decides where to branch is itself bought with branches; in long-horizon agents each pilot is a full continuation. Also: on math, placement was secondary to the advantage form.
regime: Cloned-state MuJoCo (13 envs), frozen-LLM gradient calibration, single-turn math at small scale, multi-turn Wordle (0.850 vs flat GRPO 0.790). No long-horizon tool-use agents.
information_asymmetry: The between-actions variance Var_a[Q_h(a)] exists at training time but is estimated only by paying continuations; any training-time source that predicts it without continuations (the task reference; a verifier's feedback) is unused here.
occupies: The branching objective (decision vs continuation uncertainty via the law of total variance) and the finding that placement is secondary to credit form on math.

neighbors.trick: Fork before the step where the model's own answer belief jumps most.
Fork at the most uncertain states and build a tree; mask unbranched actions.
Monte Carlo step values instead of a value network.

theme_fit.why: it is the principled objective for where to fork

limitations_as_complaints: I cannot know the between-actions variance at a state without paying for pilot continuations.
Small pilots are unreliable under sparse rewards.
